1.pericope_label: The title of the psalm, and David’s plea to be saved from the lion

schools.summary: Henry notes that the word in the title stands as a heading only here and in one prophet’s prayer, and offers two readings, a wandering song, whose several parts differ in matter and composition though artificially put together, or a charming song, very delightful. Of the Benjamite he allows that Cush may be Saul himself, whose barbarous usage of David bespoke him rather a Cushite or an Ethiopian than a true-born Israelite, but thinks it more likely some kinsman of Saul so named, an inveterate enemy who misrepresented David as a traitor and needlessly exasperated the king against him. On the two verses he numbers four pleas — David’s relation to God, his confidence in God, the rage of his enemies and the failure of all other helpers — observes that it is the glory of God to help the helpless, and adds that Paul compares Nero to a lion as David here compares Saul. Spurgeon hears the case opened with an avowal of confidence: I shake, but my rock moves not; it is never right to distrust God, and never vain to trust him. He bids us pause before we pray, lest we offer the sacrifice of fools, and hears in the dread of being torn fear co-working with faith.

Clarke derives the title from a root meaning to wander and takes it for a psalm composed in David’s wanderings, when he was obliged to hide himself from the fury of Saul; he reports Bishop Horsley’s suggestion of a wandering ode, named from its taking up different subjects in different styles, and his own alternative of an unpremeditated song, an improviso. Of Cush he finds the man unknown in Jewish history and takes the name for a disguise covering Saul, the son of Kish and of the tribe of Benjamin, judging that the subject of the psalm answers better to Saul’s unjust persecution than to anything else in David’s history.

Calvin lists the Jewish opinions on the title — a musical instrument, a tune, the opening of a common song whose air David borrowed — and prefers the second, some kind of melody or measure as one might speak of a Sapphic verse, adding that he will not contend about a matter of so small importance. On the accuser he rejects the fiction outright: David names Saul plainly elsewhere, and paints him in colours no less black than here, so why suppress the name in this place; the accuser is a real man of Saul’s tribe, either bribed by the king or currying his favour. He reads the first verse as describing David’s circumstances as a persecuted man and the second as naming the fountain of his calamity, takes the lion as setting Saul’s cruelty in a stronger light, and ascribes to God as his peculiar province the rescue of his poor sheep from the jaws of wolves.

Augustine finds the occasion not in Saul’s reign but in the later revolt of David’s son, where the friend who crossed to the son’s side to report his designs bears this name; and, reading the names spiritually rather than carnally according to the letter, he reports interpreters who render Chusi as silence, Gemini as right-handed and Achitophel as a brother’s ruin, so that the traitor Judas meets us again in the figure, since the Lord calls his disciples both sons and brethren.

Keil and Delitzsch take the heading as evidence rather than allegory: the psalm continues the confident theme of the one before it, abounds in unmistakeable references to the persecution under Saul, and carries one of those statements of occasion found only in Davidic psalms. Ellicott would render the opening claim, in thee have I taken refuge, and on the second verse notes that the poet turns from his enemies generally to the one who has just made himself conspicuous, a change from plural to singular that often occurs in the Psalms; he reports that the Greek and Latin take the verb in its primitive sense of snatch away, and notices the comparison of human enemies to beasts of prey as a reminiscence of the lion and the bear of David’s youth.

debates.question: What does the word in the title mean?

positions.view: A wandering song, its parts differing in matter and composition, or else a charming song
From a root meaning to wander: a psalm composed in David’s wanderings; or, with Horsley, a wandering ode, or an unpremeditated improviso
A kind of melody or measure, as one speaks of a Sapphic verse — but the matter is too small to contend over
Possibly Saul, whose usage of David bespoke a Cushite rather than an Israelite, but more likely a kinsman of Saul of that name
A name of disguise covering Saul himself, the son of Kish, of the tribe of Benjamin
Not Saul under a fictitious name — David names him openly elsewhere — but a real man of Saul’s tribe who slandered him
The friend of the Absalom narrative, read spiritually as silence, in a group of names figuring the betrayal of Christ

outliers.claim: Alone in referring the psalm to the later revolt rather than to Saul, and alone in reading the proper names of the title as an allegory of Judas.
Alone in arguing from David’s practice elsewhere that the title cannot be a veiled name for Saul, since David never spares him in the other psalms.

themes: Shiggaion of David, which he sang unto the Lord, concerning the words of Cush the Benjamite
O Lord my God, in thee do I put my trust: save me from all them that persecute me
Lest he tear my soul like a lion, rending it in pieces, while there is none to deliver

3.pericope_label: David’s oath of innocence, and the imprecation he calls down if it is false

schools.summary: Clarke states the charge as Saul laid it, that David was affecting the kingdom and waiting to take away the life of his king, his patron and his friend; David meets it with indignation and clears himself by an imprecation that, if he had meditated any such thing, nothing but curse and calamity might meet him from God or man. He supplies the cave: David contented himself with cutting off the skirt, merely to show the king the danger he had been in and the spirit of the man he accused of designs against his life, and even for this his heart smote him, as an indignity offered to the Lord’s anointed; the fact, with his frequent venturing of his life for the safety of the state, shows the accusations false. Wesley notes that the deliverance came when it was in David’s power to destroy him.

Keil and Delitzsch take the demonstrative to point to the substance of the Benjamite’s slanderous sayings, and set the line beside David’s own words to Saul that there is no evil in his hand, which shows in a small compass the difference between poetical and prose expression. Ellicott sees in those two notorious instances of magnanimity how closely the psalm is tied to that part of David’s life. On the verse carrying the counter-claim he reports that Ewald, on metrical grounds and to avoid the abrupt change of construction, conjectures that two clauses have dropped out, that Milton’s translation gives it another colour, and that the Greek and Latin support the supposition of corruption, so that a slight change yields the probable sense: if I have returned evil to him that dealt friendly with me, and injured my enemy without cause. On the imprecation he would read an enemy rather than the enemy, renders the verb for persecute literally as burn, and finds the word for tread used of a potter treading clay, of trampling horses and of a herd treading down its pasture; honour he takes by the parallelism for the soul or life, though to lay one’s honour in the dust is a common figure, and the pause mark he reads as a direction to the music to strike up with passion and force.

Gill observes that the crime was so public that everybody knew it and needed no particular mention, and reports the Targum turning the words upon the psalm itself: if I have made this song with an evil intention, to give an ill character of any. He notes Jarchi’s alternative rendering of the counter-claim, if I rewarded him as he rewarded me, evil for evil, which David did not; and reads the imprecation plainly, that if the charge could be proved David was content that Saul should pursue, apprehend him, and take away his life.

Spurgeon answers the charge with the record: David had suffered his enemy to escape when he had him completely in his power, twice sparing Saul’s life, once in the cave and again when he found him sleeping in the midst of his slumbering camp, and could therefore appeal to heaven with a clear conscience. He holds that he needs not fear the curse whose soul is clear of guilt, yet calls the imprecation most solemn and justifiable only through the extremity of the occasion and the dispensation the psalmist lived under, since we are now commanded to let our yea be yea, and if we cannot be believed on our word we are not to be trusted on our oath; and he warns the unconverted against trifling with imprecations, instancing the woman who wished she might die if she had not paid her share, and fell dead with the money in her hand.

debates.question: Is the text of the counter-claim sound?

positions.view: Probably corrupt: Ewald would restore two lost clauses on metrical grounds, and the Greek and Latin support the supposition
Sound as it stands, though Jarchi offers the alternative sense, if I rewarded him as he rewarded me

debates.question: May such an imprecation be imitated?

positions.view: No: it is justifiable only through the extremity of the occasion and the dispensation David lived under, since a Christian’s word should bind as another man’s oath
It was the fit instrument for clearing himself, meeting the charge with indignation and appealing to his Judge

outliers.claim: Alone in reporting the Targum’s reflexive reading, which turns the oath upon the composing of the psalm itself.
Alone in asking whether the imprecation may be copied, and in answering with a warning drawn from a recent judgment.

themes: O Lord my God, if I have done this; if there be iniquity in my hands
If I have rewarded evil unto him that was at peace with me
yea, I have delivered him that without cause is mine enemy
let the enemy persecute my soul, and take it; yea, let him tread down my life upon the earth
and lay mine honour in the dust. Selah

6.pericope_label: Arise, O Lord: the call for God to take the judgment-seat and try the hearts

schools.summary: Spurgeon makes the figure sharp: David’s sorrow makes him view the Lord as a Judge who had left the judgment-seat and retired into his rest, and the call to awake is bolder yet, implying sleep as well as inactivity and applicable to God only in a limited sense, his silence being the patience of longsuffering. At the plea for judgment he has David’s hand on an honest heart and his cry to a righteous Judge, and marvels at the closing clause: how deep the divine knowledge, how intimate the search that tries the hearts, the secret thoughts, and the reins, the inward affections. Henry sets a plea under each petition. Under the prayer for wrath he puts the enemies’ own, that they are unjustly angry at him and God may be justly angry with them, since those need not fear men’s wrath who have God’s wrath for them. The commanded judgment speaks both divine power and divine purpose: as God blesses effectually and is said to command the blessing, so he judges effectually, and though he seem to connive at wrong like one asleep he will awake in due time and make it appear that the delays were no neglects. The call to return on high he reads as a demand that God resume the royal throne whose sovereignty they had despised, noting that some make it point to the resurrection and ascension of Christ, who on returning on high had all judgment committed to him, or to his second coming.

Gill denies that local motion is meant, which cannot belong to one infinite and immense, and takes the words as spoken after the manner of men, of a God who seems sometimes to have laid himself down unconcerned, taking no notice of the insults of the wicked. On the gathering he keeps the scene national: the congregation is Israel’s twelve tribes, and he rejects the reading of several Jewish commentators who make them compass God in a hostile manner, taking it instead of Israel surrounding the altar with songs of deliverance. Of the last petition he holds that wickedness will not come to an end until the wicked are no more, since as long as they are in the world they will commit it, so that the prayer looks to a state in which there will not be a Canaanite in the house of the Lord of hosts.

Clarke reads the opening as a committal, to thee I commit my cause, arise and sit on the throne of thy judgment in my behalf; of the return on high he explains that the faithful of the land hear the charges and their minds are divided, so that for their sakes God should ascend the judgment-seat and let them see by his providence who is innocent and who guilty, an appeal David did not fear to make because the consciousness of his innocence showed him how the discrimination would be made. He asks only that his innocence be brought to light and his just dealing made clear as the noonday, and identifies the wickedness of the wicked as Saul’s own conduct. Wesley glosses the lifting up as God glorifying himself and showing himself above them, and the commanded judgment as the sentence God had appointed and declared by his prophet Samuel, adding that the people will come from all parts to worship, and that the height alludes to earthly tribunals, which are generally set up above the people.

Ellicott sees the excitement of the poet’s mind in the rapid succession of abrupt ejaculations, and would read the clause of the gathering as optative, let the communities of peoples be gathered round thee. He finds here a vision in which Jehovah summons the nations, arranges them at his tribunal and then returns to his high throne to preside — which he prefers to Delitzsch’s departure into the height as a victor after battle; and the picture of arraigned nations he holds to favour making the psalm the voice of the community rather than of an individual. On the plea of innocence he reports Jerome’s refusal of it to David at all, as belonging properly to the sinless Saviour, and the view of others that the ideal Israel stands at the tribunal; but he compares Job’s protestations of innocence and persistent demand for a trial, and holds that David refers to his innocence of the charge calumniously brought, since as between Saul and himself his conduct had been blameless. He glosses the word for establish as let him stand erect, and notes that the verb for try is used of testing metals. Keil and Delitzsch hear in the strophe the calm language of courageous trust, and insist the prayer is directed not against the individuals as such but against the wickedness in them, which makes this psalm the key to all psalms containing prayers against enemies.

debates.question: Whose plea of innocence is this?

positions.view: Not David’s at all: Jerome holds it belongs properly to the sinless Saviour, and others to the ideal Israel; but David may say it of this charge, his conduct towards Saul having been blameless
David’s own, asking that his innocence be brought to light and his just dealing made clear as the noonday

debates.question: Who are the congregation that compass God about?

positions.view: The nations, summoned and arraigned at the tribunal — a picture favouring the psalm as the voice of the community
Israel’s twelve tribes surrounding the altar with songs of deliverance, not compassing God in a hostile manner as several Jewish commentators read it
The people coming from all parts to worship and offer praises and sacrifices

outliers.claim: Alone in making the psalm a hermeneutical key, on the ground that its prayer is aimed at the wickedness in the enemies rather than at the enemies themselves.
Alone in pressing how far the language of waking God may be taken, and in answering that it applies to him only in a limited sense.

themes: Arise, O Lord, in thine anger, lift up thyself because of the rage of mine enemies
awake for me to the judgment that thou hast commanded
So shall the congregation of the people compass thee about: for their sakes therefore return thou on high
Judge me, O Lord, according to my righteousness, and according to mine integrity that is in me
for the righteous God trieth the hearts and reins

10.pericope_label: God my shield, the daily anger against the wicked, and the whetted sword

schools.summary: Henry hears in the opening an exclusive claim: not merely that God is his defender, but that he looks for defence in no other, his hope of shelter in danger being placed in God alone; on that he builds two confidences, that God saves the upright in heart with an everlasting salvation and that he owns every righteous cause. Reading the wicked’s doom in the sanctuary, he finds them not to be envied, since as God’s mercies are new every morning towards his people, so his anger is new every morning against the wicked, upon the fresh occasions their renewed transgressions give; and he is angry with them even in the merriest of their days, and in the days of their devotion, for if they prosper it is in wrath, and if they pray their very prayers are an abomination. Spurgeon adds that God not only detests sin but is angry with those who continue to indulge in it, for we have no insensible and stolid God to deal with.

Ellicott reads the Hebrew literally as my shield is upon God, comparing a place where the same construction makes God the shield-bearer. He knows the versions that soften the next line and the proposal to read and not for and God, but judges the change unnecessary, the two clauses answering to each other. He calls the Hebrew of the warning doubly idiomatic and would render it surely, he will again whet his sword, notes that bent is literally trodden, the foot being used to bend the bow as archers use it still, and reads the instruments of death as arrows tipped with fire by wrapping them in burning tow. Keil and Delitzsch hold that if God will in the end let his wrath break forth, he will not do it without having threatened it every day, making the ungodly feel his indignation beforehand to strike a wholesome terror into them; the subject of the condition is any ungodly person whatever, and of the main clause God, so that if a man does not repent the Lord will whet his sword.

Clarke fights out the chapter’s textual battle at length. He traces the sentence about daily anger through the Chaldee, Vulgate, Greek, Syriac, Arabic and Ethiopic, and through Coverdale, Cardmarden and the Genevan version, observing that the evidence on one side positively affirms that God is angry every day and on the other positively denies it, the mass of it supporting the denial. The corruption he lays at the Chaldee’s door, for adding the words with the wicked, which the English translators followed while printing them in italics as absent from the Hebrew; and since the same letters pointed one way mean God and pointed the other mean not, he would restore the sense as God judgeth the righteous, and is not angry every day — he is not always chiding, which is why several versions bring in patience and longsuffering. Of the weapons he takes the instruments of death for a prophecy of Saul’s tragical death, wounded by Philistine arrows and ending his woful days on his own keen sword.

Gill prefers my shield is with God, and takes the shield for Christ, now with the Father as intercessor and advocate, opposing his blood and righteousness to all the accusations of Satan. He guards the other clause, that not all who are thought righteous are such, nor is any man naturally righteous or righteous by his own obedience, but only those made so by the obedience of Christ. Of the warning he insists the one who must turn is not God but the wicked man, who must repent until a change is wrought in his heart and life, and notes that the Greek, Latin, Arabic and Ethiopic read if ye turn not, as an apostrophe to the wicked.

debates.question: Is God angry with the wicked every day?

positions.view: The text says not: the mass of the versions deny it, the Chaldee corrupted the verse by adding with the wicked, and a change of pointing restores God judgeth the righteous, and is not angry every day
The received reading stands; the proposal to read and not for and God is unnecessary, the two clauses answering to each other
He is angry every day, his anger as new each morning against the wicked as his mercies are towards his people

debates.question: Who is the one that must turn?

positions.view: The wicked man, who must repent until a change is wrought in heart and life; the Greek and Latin read it as an address to the wicked
Any ungodly person whatever is the subject of the condition, and God of the clause that follows
Surely, he will again whet his sword — the Hebrew being doubly idiomatic

outliers.claim: Alone in collating nine versions and three English Bibles against the received text, and in concluding that the familiar clause about daily anger is a Chaldee corruption.
Alone in identifying the shield with Christ as present intercessor rather than with divine protection in general.

themes: My defence is of God, which saveth the upright in heart
God judgeth the righteous, and God is angry with the wicked every day
If he turn not, he will whet his sword; he hath bent his bow, and made it ready
He hath also prepared for him the instruments of death; he ordaineth his arrows against the persecutors

14.pericope_label: The mischief that miscarries, the pit that takes its digger, and the closing praise

schools.summary: Henry gives the figure as a false conception: the sinner’s head conceives the mischief, contrives it with art and keeps the plot close, while his heart travails with iniquity; but at the birth it proves falsehood, a cheat upon himself, a lie in his right hand, for he cannot compass what he intended, nor, gaining his point, gain the satisfaction he promised himself. Of the pit he generalises that all sinners prepare destruction for themselves by preparing themselves for destruction. The closing righteousness he takes to cover both halves of the psalm, the glory of that gracious protection under which God takes his afflicted people and of the just vengeance with which he will pursue those who afflict them, sung to the Lord most high, who, when his enemies deal proudly, shows he is above them. Spurgeon traces the parentage instead: the devil has had doings with the man and the virus of evil is in him, so the child is worthy of its father, whose name of old was the father of lies. He notices what the work cost the digger, who stooped to the dirty work and did not fear to soil his hands, willing to work in a ditch if others might fall therein; such men hunt the godly as brute beasts, and will not give them the fair chase afforded the hare or the fox, but must secretly entrap them, being able neither to run them down nor shoot them down. He ends on the contrast, the bright jewel sparkling in a black foil, and leaves the slandered man a singer again, his harp unstrung for a little season and now sweeping its chords.

Clarke takes the metaphor of the pit from pits dug in the earth and slightly covered with reeds, so as not to be discerned from solid ground, until the animal steps on them, the surface breaks, and he falls in; Saul laid his plans with artifice and executed them with zeal, and when he had, as he supposed, David’s grave digged, he fell in himself. He quotes Horne, that all the world acknowledges the equity of a sentence which inflicts on the guilty the punishment they intended for the innocent. He glosses the old word for the head as the scalp or crown, thinks it may refer to knocking a criminal on the head to deprive him of life, and adds that had scalping been known then he should have thought that barbarous custom was meant. At the close he celebrates both justice and mercy, takes the name for the perfections of a Jehovah above all, and quotes the old Scotico-English psalter beginning here, that song falls to joy, and he who sings that name well has joy more than can be told. Wesley reads the travail as deep design and vigorous endeavour, restless till the mischief is accomplished.

Gill keeps to the pain, that the man is big with iniquity as a woman with child, uneasy till he commits it, and that he digged his pit large and capacious to answer his purposes. He has what the man devised against others fall upon himself, as a just judgment from heaven. The closing praise he grounds in a precedent: righteousness displayed in vindicating the innocent and punishing the wicked, as when the king who ordered the Hebrew infants drowned was himself drowned with his host, and Israel sang.

Ellicott draws the principle that God’s judgments are not arbitrary but follow on sin as its consequence, the verb for travail giving the general figure which the two following clauses elaborate. He notes the English word for the head is one retained from Coverdale and common in the Elizabethan age, and records that Eusebius applied these verses to the overthrow of Maxentius by Constantine, who in preparing a bridge of boats had prepared the means of his own destruction.

debates.question: How far does the self-destruction of the wicked reach?

positions.view: To all sinners, who prepare destruction for themselves by preparing themselves for destruction
To Saul in particular: the grave he dug for David took him instead
It is a standing principle, God’s judgments following on sin as its natural consequence, and already applied in history to the fall of Maxentius

outliers.claim: Alone in carrying the pit forward into church history, by way of the bridge of boats on which Maxentius perished.
Alone in pausing over the archaeology of the word for the head, and in quoting a mediaeval Scottish psalter on the closing verse.

themes: Behold, he travaileth with iniquity, and hath conceived mischief, and brought forth falsehood
He made a pit, and digged it, and is fallen into the ditch which he made
His mischief shall return upon his own head, and his violent dealing shall come down upon his own pate
I will praise the Lord according to his righteousness: and will sing praise to the name of the Lord most high
